title: The Guardian view on humanities cuts in universities: academic departments are more than cost centres | Editorial
summary:

“I ask nothing more from you than to do what you have been doing. Go out into the fray and keep reading,” was Percival Everett’s advice when he addressed graduating students at Wesleyan university in Connecticut last summer. Fitting words from a prize-winning novelist, at a time when gambling has become a more common leisure activity in the US than reading a book. In the UK, too, concerns are growing about the decline of reading, partly due to ubiquitous screen-based entertainment. Last week, parliament’s education committee called for the National Year of Reading to be extended to a decade, to inculcate the habit in children and young people.

All academic disciplines use books to convey information, but for literature and the humanities more widely, they are an indispensable currency. As the 2026 graduation season draws to a close, and robes and mortarboards are put away for another year, there is growing anger that these subjects are under attack from university administrations looking for ways to save money – while ministers look away.

Analysis of 2024 data for the Guardian uncovered nearly 4,000 job cuts in Shape (the acronym for social sciences, humanities and arts). All but 110 were in non-Russell Group universities, which have lower entry requirements and recruit more socioeconomically disadvantaged students, leading to concerns that some courses might become the preserve of an elite. But humanities cuts are not limited to one type of institution. Exeter plans to cut 150 full-time posts. Nottingham expects to become the first Russell Group university to withdraw all its modern foreign language degrees.

Prof Susan J Smith, president of the British Academy, recently described the situation as “an emergency, threatening all subjects”, and singled out the problem of “cold spots” where some disciplines are at risk of disappearing. It is not clear that the review of higher education which the academy wants would provide a solution. But she is right to highlight the negative effects of fragmented decision-making. To accountants, some courses or departments may be viewed as cost centres. But to lecturers and students, and the places in which they are based, they are cultural resources – repositories of knowledge built up over decades, some of which will have a specific, local character and relevance.

No one argues that no course should ever close. But the choices that students make are partly driven by changes further down the education system. The rising popularity of Stem (science, technology, engineering and maths) is partly due to the Conservative policy of promoting them; the fall in teenagers opting for literature is linked to an unimaginative GCSE (surely something that a new prime minister with an English degree could fix).

Universities make their own decisions about what and who to teach. But ministers must be upfront about the constraints in which they operate. An expected £100m cut to teaching grants, combined with the introduction of an international student levy, mean that a years-long financial squeeze is set to carry on. In such a climate, standing up for the value of literature and the humanities ought not to be left to famous novelists.

title: Education researchers warn political review of federal grants could reshape what gets studied
summary:
The research behind the influential “science of reading” movement was built over decades through federally supported research spanning cognitive science, neuroscience, psychology, linguistics and classroom studies. The post Education researchers warn political review of federal grants could reshape what gets studied appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
The research behind the influential “science of reading” movement was built over decades through federally supported research spanning cognitive science, neuroscience, psychology, linguistics and classroom studies.

Education research organizations say a proposed 100-page sweeping overhaul of federal grant rules, which would add a new review by political appointees, could make it harder to produce similar important bodies of evidence in the future.

The federal Office of Management and Budget (OMB) says its proposed changes are intended to strengthen accountability, transparency and oversight of taxpayer-funded grants. The May 29 proposal would revise the rules for issuing and overseeing grants, including those awarded by the Department of Education and the National Science Foundation, two major sources of federal education research funding. OMB wants the final rule to take effect by Oct. 1, according to the proposal.

But in letters submitted to OMB on July 13, the deadline for public comment, education research groups argued that some provisions could have unintended and harmful consequences by narrowing the questions researchers study, giving political considerations too much influence in funding decisions and disrupting research already underway. The education groups are asking not only for changes, but for the entire overhaul proposal to be withdrawn.

Objections specific to education research were detailed in three letters from the National Academy of Education, signed by 19 other education and science organizations; the American Educational Research Association (AERA); and the Knowledge Alliance, a group representing about 20 organizations that conduct education research.

Could researchers study differences in student outcomes?

One of the most significant concerns raised by education researchers involves studies that examine whether educational outcomes differ among student groups.

The proposed rule would prohibit federal funds from supporting research related to what the administration calls “unlawful diversity, equity and inclusion” activities and would restrict funding for what are known as “disparate impact studies.” These analyze whether policies that might appear neutral produce different results for different groups.

The National Academy of Education, in a letter signed by 19 other education and science organizations, warned that the rule could ban studies examining racial or ethnic achievement gaps, and whether educational interventions help some students more than others.

“Whether a reading intervention works differently for English language learners, whether a discipline policy falls more heavily on students of color, whether a gifted education program under-identifies students with disabilities — these are not fringe questions,” the organization wrote. “They are central empirical questions of education policy research.”

Researchers also pointed to possible conflicts with existing education laws and programs that require demographic analysis. For example, the roughly $17 billion federal program for high-poverty schools known as Title I requires states and districts to examine student outcomes by race, disability status, income and English learner status in order to identify and support struggling groups of students.

The proposed rule does not explicitly prohibit all such analysis. But researchers argue that the language around diversity, equity and inclusion and “disparate impact” is broad and vague enough to create uncertainty and discourage researchers from proposing important studies.

Who decides what counts as valuable research?

Education researchers also object to proposed changes that would increase political involvement in grant decisions.

The proposal would require agencies to consider alignment with federal priorities, which could change from administration to administration, and the “national interest,” which is undefined. It also states that political appointees are to review all grants before they are issued. Research organizations argue that this requirement could reduce the role of independent scientific review, when subject experts evaluate proposals based on quality, rigor and feasibility.

Researchers also worry that the Trump administration’s push for “gold standard science” in the proposal is undefined and could favor some methods over others. Education research is not as straightforward as testing the effectiveness of a new drug and often uses a variety of approaches — including surveys, interviews and sophisticated data analysis that attempt to replicate an experiment without randomly assigning students to a program or a style of instruction.

Among other changes, the OMB proposal calls upon agencies to give preference to grant proposals with low overhead costs, which disadvantages large research universities. It would also cut federal funding for attending conferences and publication costs, unless specifically approved. Researchers would be required to provide written justification for each request to receive grant funds, adding to their regulatory paperwork. Education research organizations objected to all of these proposals.

The White House proposal emphasizes supporting research that can yield immediate results or breakthrough innovations. In response, the Knowledge Alliance pointed to the science of reading as an example of why real progress requires patience.

“Researchers would be less likely to pursue important long-term questions that are critical to creating the foundational knowledge needed for scientific breakthroughs,” wrote Rachel Dinkes, president of the Knowledge Alliance. The science of reading “reflects the accumulation of evidence over many years and across multiple administrations, which has been pivotal to improving student outcomes in reading.”

What happens when research is interrupted?

Education research groups also raised concerns about the consequences of suspending or terminating grants after studies have begun.

The National Academy of Education warned that interruptions could be especially damaging for longitudinal studies, which depend on consistent data collection over time. Losing a year of data collection, the group argued, could permanently damage a study’s value.

Researchers also pointed to effects beyond universities. Federal research grants often fund partnerships between researchers and schools, provide professional learning or pay for interventions for students. The consequences of abrupt terminations are fresh in education researchers’ minds. When the Department of Education terminated dozens of research studies in 2025, for example, 1,600 high schoolers with disabilities lost services.

Restrictions on international research partnerships were another concern. Researchers argued that broad limits on foreign collaborations could affect U.S. participation in international assessments such as PISA and TIMSS, which help policymakers compare U.S. student performance with that of other countries.

The Trump administration’s proposal to overhaul how the federal government awards and oversees grants is drawing fierce opposition from scientific societies and research organizations across many fields, from medicine to climate science. These comments from the education research community are just three among 496,775 that have been submitted. A July 14 article in MedPage Today explained that research organizations intentionally flooded the OMB with comments to respond to, hoping to either slow the rule-making process or create an administrative record that could be used in future lawsuits to challenge the rule.

OMB did not respond to questions about the objections raised by education researchers.

title: Do You Have to Be Fancy to Get Published in ‘Science’?
summary:
Do You Have to Be Fancy to Get Published in ‘Science’?
kathryn.palmer… Mon, 07/20/2026 - 03:00 AM

No, not necessarily. But scientists who work for a prestigious university are three times more likely than their peers who don’t to get published in the top-tier journal, according to a new independent analysis of Science’s manuscript data.

Byline(s)
Kathryn Palmer
full_text:
It’s no secret that it’s harder than ever to get published in a top scientific journal.

Faculty remain under the age-old pressure to publish or perish, especially in big-name journals that carry the most influence with tenure and promotion committees, other scientists, and public policymakers. Meanwhile, submissions are at an all-time high, in part because generative AI has helped ramp up the production of papers (of varying quality). One analysis shows that the number of articles indexed in the Web of Science database increased by 47 percent—from 1.7 million to 2.5 million—between 2015 and 2024, far outpacing the growth of the scientific workforce.

That competition also translates to low acceptance rates at top-tier peer-reviewed journals, which range between 5 and 8 percent at Science, Nature, the New England Journal of Medicine and the American Economic Review.

A quick scan of the authors who do manage to get published suggests that a disproportionate share work at selective, wealthy universities.

“When you read articles published in Science or Nature, you see all the famous institutions represented there,” Aaron Clauset, a computer science professor at the University of Colorado, told Inside Higher Ed. “It doesn’t take a high-tech study to see that there’s a correlation between institutional prestige and journal prestige in terms of publishing.”

Prestige Bias?

But little data was available for researchers to independently analyze that metric or any other characteristics of successful authors—until now.

Earlier this year, the American Association for the Advancement of Science gave Clauset and his team unprecedented access to anonymized data from 110,303 manuscripts submitted between 2015 and 2020 to two of its journals, Science and Science Advances. Just as his team sought to “understand how to make the scientific peer-review system more meritocratic by examining where the potential biases might be,” Clauset said, AAAS was “very interested in essentially doing an audit of their own process to understand: Are they being biased? Are there places where they can do better?”

According to the resulting analysis published in Science Advances last week, getting published in Science—which accepted about 6 percent of submissions between 2015 and 2020—or its sister publication Science Advances—which accepted about 10.5 percent of submissions—tends to be easier for scientists with certain characteristics.

For example, manuscripts by authors from the most prestigious institutions had an 11.6 percent acceptance rate, compared to 3.4 percent for those from the least prestigious institutions. (Researchers created an algorithm linked to university rankings to determine prestige levels.)

Although researchers were careful to note that correlation doesn’t equate to causation, the findings raise questions for future analysis: “Is it simply the case that the elite institutions are doing the best work and that the elite journals are just publishing the best work?” Clauset said. “Or is it the case that there may be a prestige bias in the system in which maybe authors from elite institutions are given more of the benefit of the doubt in terms of how their work is evaluated?”

In addition to a possible prestige bias, researchers identified numerous other factors—including research topic, national origin and gender—associated with higher acceptance rates. According to the paper, Science published 9.6 percent of submissions on research focused on viruses, infection, RNA and immune response, but only 1.7 percent of research more focused on how science intersects with politics, economics, gender and the societal dimensions of COVID.

Papers from large teams, with 10 or more authors, were accepted at three times the rate of those produced by small teams, with one to five authors. Papers with authors from the United States or Canada were accepted at 3.3 times the rate of authors based in China. And U.S.-based authors with Chinese last names had lower acceptance rates than their U.S.-based peers without Chinese last names. Women were also at a slight disadvantage, with the journals accepting 5.3 percent of papers written by women compared to 6.4 percent written by men.

At the same time, “bias is difficult to identify separately from quality from these data,” the authors of the study wrote.

“The prestige and team size associations likely reflect a combination of status signaling effects and resource advantages among elite institutions and larger teams that may independently improve manuscript quality,” the study reads. “The high volume of submissions [from authors based in China] may reflect a region-specific incentive to submit work to high-impact journals regardless of suitability, such as China’s past publication bounty program. Editors then rebalance the submission pool to filter these out during editorial review.”

While getting published in a peer-reviewed journal is a multistep process, much of the rejection happens early on. The study found that editors at Science rejected 83 percent of submissions and roughly 75 percent of submissions to Science Advances before ever sending them out for peer review.

However, the qualities associated with higher author success rates “aren’t concentrated at one step of the peer-review process,” said Sam Zhang, an assistant professor of mathematics and statistics at University of Vermont and co-author of the study. “Across the board, both the editors and the reviewers’ [decisions on what to publish] are correlated with these author characteristics.”

As far as Zhang knows, this may be the first time a journal of Science’s influence has released such a large set of manuscript data for independent review. And he’s hopeful that publication of the findings “will be a watershed moment for the publishing ecosystem” and inspire more journals to release similar data. “If every single journal released its manuscript data and one journal’s publications skewed toward one demographic category or another, it would help scientists pinpoint deeper biases.”

And the urgency for influential scientific journals to make sure they’re publishing the best science—not just research affiliated with the biggest names—may be greater than ever in the age of AI.

“The role of elite journals in the ecosystem might become more important as the barrier to entry becomes lower,” Zhang said. “Scientists need some way of filtering the vast amounts of information that they receive. Traditional status symbols like a journal’s reputation are very helpful heuristics for many working scientists to decide what to read.”

As AI increases the broader scientific literature’s volume, he added, “understanding what drives acceptance in these journals might only become more important.”

(This story has been updated to more accurately reflect the relationship between Science and Science Advances.)

title: Driving More Students to ‘High-Value’ Programs
summary:
Driving More Students to ‘High-Value’ Programs
Doug Lederman Mon, 07/20/2026 - 03:00 AM

Defining programs solely by graduates’ earnings isn’t ideal, but it’s where we are. A new report shows that it can be done, and how.

Byline(s)
Doug Lederman
full_text:
Higher education’s access era ran from the 1960s through the ’90s, as the Higher Education Act and Pell Grant encouraged colleges and universities to better live up to their promise to open doors to opportunity for all. The focus shifted to completion in the 2000s and early 2010s, driven by Lumina Foundation’s “big goal” and the Obama administration’s belief that postsecondary learning was valuable and that college without a credential could have disastrous consequences.

Over the last decade-plus, we embraced an emphasis on student success, defined by a broader definition of well-being and more focus on colleges’ own responsibility to help individual learners reach their goals in and outside the classroom.

The last few years have seen another pivot, to the era of value, as a powerful combination of higher education’s continuing unaffordability and a drastically changing workplace drove deeper questions about whether college was “worth it.” These doubts have been reinforced by better federal and state data to measure the economic payoff of individual programs and credentials.

Let’s put aside for the moment very legitimate questions (which I’ve raised before) about whether it’s wise to measure the value of any academic experience exclusively based on what those who’ve been through it earn financially a few years later. (My short answer is no: As I wrote in January, “overdependence on postcollege economic outcomes to judge higher education’s success and value ignores the full range of benefits that colleges and universities purport to deliver for individuals and for society collectively.” It also shortchanges the value of programs like social work and theology and the arts that tend to produce graduates for historically low-paying fields.)

But if inadequate on their own, economic outcomes are an absolutely appropriate way to judge a postsecondary experience, and now that governments and others are using postcollege earnings as a metric, colleges and universities have to get with the program.

But how? What can and should institutions do to better ensure that their learners are prepared for, get and succeed in jobs or experiences they enter after college? Isn’t that heavily dependent on the kinds of students they serve, the (good and bad) choices those learners make, the shape of their local economies, and other factors outside their control?

To some extent yes—but, really, tough beans. While we can work to improve accountability systems based on earnings and develop alternative ones using additional factors, some of our focus right now has to be on figuring out how to better meet the requirements (and, let’s be real, to better serve students).

I’ll focus in this column on one such effort: the Unlocking Opportunity project from the Aspen Institute’s College Excellence Program and the Community College Research Center at Columbia University’s Teachers College. Aspen and CCRC are far from alone in working in this space (see complementary work from places like the Urban Institute and HCM Strategists, among others), but their strategy is notable in several ways.

First, it brought a cohort of institutions together in 2022, comparatively early in the march toward embedding value measures into accountability regimes, so the initiative has several years’ worth of results and data to work with.

Second, the effort focuses on community colleges, extremely important institutions that can struggle to meet accountability metrics because they open their doors to virtually all comers and many learners don’t seek credentials. Some community college leaders, for instance, have been frustrated by the fact that about a fifth of two-year institutions have been labeled as “low earnings” colleges by the new Carnegie Classification on Student Access and Outcomes.

Accountability measures like the new federal Do No Harm standard are unlikely to be a sufficient motivator for colleges to get serious about increasing the value of their programs because they set such a low floor; fewer than 2 percent of bachelor’s degree programs and about 7 percent of associate degree programs would fail to meet the new federal threshold if it were in effect now.

“But if we in higher education are in the business of continuous improvement, there’s no excuse for not doing something to improve value,” says Josh Wyner, founder and executive director of Aspen’s College Excellence Program. “It’s the right thing to do for students and society.”

More than a third of community college credentials, including certificates, are unlikely to lead directly to good jobs or bachelor’s degrees that open doors to good jobs, the Unlocking Opportunity report notes.

The goal of the consortium, which began with a pilot group of 10 community colleges and now has 54 more, is to have more students enroll in and complete high-value programs and fewer enter programs unlikely to lead to postgraduation success. The vision is that institutions do this not once, to meet an accountability threshold, but open-endedly.

The first step was developing a definition of value that doesn’t strive for perfection but is “close enough to drive institutional reform behavior in a positive way,” Wyner says. To judge the value of programs that are designed to lead to a job directly after community college, Aspen and CCRC use postcompletion earnings. For programs designed to lead to a job only after transfer to a four-year institution and attainment of a bachelor’s degree, the initiative defines value by a mix of transfer rates, bachelor’s completion rates and “individualized program mapping between community colleges and their four-year counterparts.”

The 10 colleges in the pilot then divided all of their programs into categories (high, medium or low-value workforce programs, high or low-value transfer programs, etc.) and developed strategies for increasing enrollments in high-value programs and reducing enrollments in lower-value ones.

In the first three years of work, the 10 colleges collectively increased the number of students in high-value programs or pathways by 27 percent (roughly 20,000 students) and decreased enrollment in low-value courses of study by 25 percent (about 7,500).

The institutions used two major tactics to achieve these results: strengthening the labor market value of workforce programs and improving advising for potential transfer students. But the tactics varied by institution.

Southwest Wisconsin Technical College required leaders of 11 workforce programs that typically paid graduates less than a living wage to figure out how raise that level. The college changed the curriculum for its agronomy program, for example, to include drone certification and a course in pesticide application after employers said they’d pay $2.50 more an hour to workers with those skills. The college closed two culinary programs and an automotive-collision course that couldn’t successfully adapt or local employers wouldn’t cooperate. The result: an 84 percent decrease in enrollments in low-value programs and a 32 percent increase in high- or medium-value programs.

St. Petersburg College found that too many of its students were in a general associate of arts program that did not require focused advising. It embedded career advising and earlier and more structured conversations about transfer pathways and over three years produced a 37 percent increase in the number of students in high-value transfer programs and a 47 percent decrease in those in low-value transfer programs.

Aspen and CCRC plan to expand the lessons and strategies from the pilot to dozens of additional community colleges and, potentially, to four-year institutions as well.

But all the strategies and good practices in the world won’t matter unless institutional leaders—and the faculty and staff members who will have to do the heavy lifting—embrace the idea that they have a responsibility to do what they can to improve the postcollege outcomes of their learners. Public policy and accountability requirements won’t necessarily force them to do it, because the bars they set are so low. Recognizing that we’ve entered a new era—that this is what learners need from us in this moment—is the first step.

title: How Soon Could Colleges Lose Loan Access Under New Accountability Metric?
summary:
How Soon Could Colleges Lose Loan Access Under New Accountability Metric?
jessica.blake@… Mon, 07/20/2026 - 03:00 AM

For most programs, data from the new test on student earnings will be released in 2027 and failing programs could face penalties in 2028. But some have been granted an extension that student advocates say is harmful.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
Initial data showing which college programs pass and fail a new student earnings test is slated to be released at some point in 2027. The first round of programmatic penalties based on the data won’t kick in until 2028—and only for some.

The Education Department finalized the metric, known as the Do No Harm test, last month. The end goal of the program is to more equally hold all colleges accountable for the outcomes of their students. It does so by cutting off access to federal loans for low-earning degree programs. (In rare cases, colleges could lose access to the Pell Grant, too.) Under the law that created the metric, the department must publish data for at least two years before the sanction kicks in. And now, critics worry that an exception for certain programs could even further delay that penalty, undermining the initial purpose of the test.

Here’s how the earnings metric works.

Each year, federal data collected by the Education Department and the Internal Revenue Service will be used to compare the earnings of college students four years after they graduate to those of adults with only a high school diploma. If an undergraduate program’s average graduate does not earn more than the high school diploma holder, then the program fails. (The same is true for graduate programs, but the comparison is to an adult with just a bachelor’s degree.)

When Congress established the Do No Harm test in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, it explicitly wrote that the department must wait until a program had failed the test in two out of three consecutive years before enforcing the penalty, likely to provide a buffer for anomalies in the earnings data. What lawmakers did not direct the department to do was delay the penalty for programs that lead to careers reliant on tip-based income, but that’s the case under the department’s final regulations.

The department originally planned to treat those programs—which include cosmetology, culinary arts and massage therapy—the same as any other. The government would use existing data from 2025 to run the first round of earnings tests, and the results would be posted in 2027. But lobbyists representing the tip-based fields—many of which fall among those with the highest predicted failure rates—wrote in comments to the department that the 2025 IRS tax-form data wasn’t accurate.

When individuals fill out their tax forms, it’s an honor system, and not everyone maintains integrity when doing so, the lobbyists argued. So, if individuals underreport their tips or fail to report them at all, it could disadvantage the programs they graduated from on the earnings test.

The solution, the service industry lobbyists said, was to wait a year. Starting in 2026, tips won’t be taxed under a new law, which industry leaders believe will lead to more accurate self-reporting and a fairer earnings test. But that data won’t come out until 2027 and can’t be cleaned, analyzed and released until 2028—and that’s when lobbyists argue the tallying should start.

In the end, the Education Department acquiesced.

“After considering the totality of feedback … received on the issue of unreported and under-reported tipped income, the department has decided to delay the implementation of the accountability framework for certain programs,” officials wrote in the final rule.

So now, while the first round of data from the earnings test will be released for all programs in 2027, it will only count toward the two-out-of-three-years penalty for some. And though some programs could lose access to loans as early as 2028, the consequence won’t hit programs in 20 tip-reliant fields like cosmetology until at least 2029. (If a degree program is small and the department doesn’t have enough data from one graduating class to randomly select a sample and protect students’ data privacy, it may have to wait yet another year.)

But critics, many of whom are from student-centered research and policy groups, say the change just delays the inevitable for poor-performing programs.

An analysis by the Postsecondary Education and Economics Research Center at American University shows that programs in the 20 categories enroll 39 percent of the students who receive federal aid and are enrolled in programs that fail the minimum earnings test. A separate PEER study found that underreporting of tips only accounts for about 8 percent of earnings in personal services fields.

“The administration is showing its true colors with this delay,” said Clare McCann, managing director of policy at PEER and a former Education Department official during the Biden administration. “Adding a year—or more—before these favored programs see any consequence for leaving their graduates with extremely low earnings does nothing more than punt on the goals of accountability and waste taxpayer dollars and students’ time and money.”

The department itself noted in the final regulations that “the issue of under-reported tipped income is likely to be much smaller than what some commenters suggested.” It also said that though the no-tax-on-tips policy is set to expire after tax year 2028, the tip-based programs will not regain exemption from the earnings test, nor will it factor in additional industry-collected data on tips.

“This is an unacceptable outcome,” wrote Jeremy Bauer-Wolf, investigations manager at New America, a left-leaning think tank. “Postponing sanctions could mean that schools that are failing students may never be held to account.”

Bauer-Wolf and McCann are not alone in their concern. Congressional Democrats like Sen. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois introduced a bill last week that would block the department from providing the extension to tip-based programs, among other things that raise the bar when it comes to holding programs accountable.

Still, tip-dependent programs say the delay is about making things fair.

“We think it’s a pretty significant amount [20 to 30 percent] of total income [that] gets underreported in the current system, and so the hope is by seeing no tax on tips come into play, we’ll see more accurate reporting and a better reflection of the true earning potential of individuals who come through our schools, complete the programs, pass their licensing exams and then get out into the world and get jobs,” said John Russell, executive director at the American Association of Career Schools, a national nonprofit that represents privately owned beauty and massage therapy schools. “There’s a fundamental fairness to asking for accurate data.”

And even with the timeline change, some lobbying groups argue it’s not enough.

“We are pleased that, for the first time, all institutions of higher education will be held accountable to the same standards,” said Jordan Wicker, senior vice president of legislative and regulatory affairs at Career Education Colleges and Universities, an association representing for-profit colleges. That said, “we remain concerned that the new earnings formula fails to address important factors affecting wages, such as part-time work, gender pay disparities and regional income variations, [and] we are hopeful that some of these issues can be resolved in future modifications.”

title: Tell Your Enrollment Story Before Someone Else Does
summary:
Tell Your Enrollment Story Before Someone Else Does
Elizabeth Redden Mon, 07/20/2026 - 03:00 AM

If colleges and universities don’t act now to explain their admission decisions, they will be vulnerable to political attacks.

Byline(s)
Sean Robins
full_text:
In the coming months, data from the federal government’s new Admissions and Consumer Transparency Supplement survey—which collects seven years’ worth of detailed admission and enrollment data from U.S. colleges and universities—is expected to be published. When it is, it will renew debate about how colleges decide who gets admitted and who doesn’t.

The National Association for College Admission Counseling and many higher education organizations are concerned about ACTS. Colleges had very little time to gather their data, and in many cases, the data is incomplete because reporting policies vary across institutions. Federal courts even questioned the legality of ACTS: In April, a federal judge issued two separate preliminary injunctions blocking the federal government from requiring it in 17 states or for universities that are party to the ongoing litigation.

Regardless, colleges and universities must prepare for the ACTS data to shape public conversation about admission and enrollment for years to come. That is why it is critical that institutions tell their enrollment stories now. Here are some steps colleges can take.

Document Everything

What factors shaped your enrollment strategy, and how does that connect to your institution’s mission and purpose? Did you admit students to help meet a particular workforce need? Did your institution commit to enrolling local students to help serve your state’s interests? Document these factors.

Prepare Across Departments

Don’t let conflicting information undermine your credibility. Admissions, institutional research, communications, government relations and campus leadership must align to consistently communicate how enrollment decisions are made and how they support your institution’s broader objectives.

Inform Your Publics

Create a plan to communicate your admission story to your key stakeholders. There’s already increased attention on admission and enrollment from policymakers, regulators and the media, and this will only increase when ACTS is released. Stakeholders will want to know what happened and, more importantly, why. Institutions that wait until questions arise may find themselves reacting to narratives created by others.

For many colleges and universities, this level of storytelling is a shift. Transparency is being demanded from higher education institutions like never before, and those that will navigate this changing environment best will be the ones that articulate and explain their decisions. Without storytelling, institutions risk others coming to their own conclusions.

Too often, admission is portrayed as an overly simplified process of selecting students with the highest grades and test scores. In reality, it is far more complex.

Colleges and universities are mission-driven institutions. They serve distinct student populations, pursue unique objectives and respond to the needs of their communities in different ways. A community college, a regional public university, a land-grant institution and a highly selective research university enroll differently because their missions and responsibilities vary considerably.

Consider this: An institution might have expanded its nursing and teacher-education programs to address workforce shortages, requiring it to recruit more students who wish to pursue those paths. Another may have invested in undergraduate research opportunities, or committed to serving in-state students from low-income regions to help meet a state priority of uplifting its most vulnerable residents.

Factors like these influence admission decisions every year. That’s why data alone can’t tell the whole story.

Higher education is the most powerful pathway to opportunity in the U.S. Research shows that college graduates, on average, earn roughly $1.2 million more in their lifetimes compared to high school graduates. Yet, confidence in our colleges and universities cannot be taken for granted. Trust is built when they explain their work, answer difficult questions and help the public better understand how they operate.

The release of ACTS data will generate conversation, skepticism and debate. Institutions cannot control every narrative that emerges from it. They can, however, ensure that they are clearly communicating facts grounded in purpose and what their data does and does not show.

Now is the time to tell your story.

title: Inside the horrifying online network where children extort others to commit violence and self-harm
summary:
The 764 network is just one part of a growing online ecosystem that pushes young members into brutal and degrading acts. It has perpetrators and victims in dozens of countries

full_text:
In late 2024, in a quiet suburb of Stockholm, a 14-year-old boy approached a man in his 80s who was using a walker. He stabbed the man three times in the back.

The video of the attack in Hässelby was streamed and spread quickly. It fed a global online ecosystem that actively encourages and glorifies acts of violence and degradation – the “gamification of harm”, as the researcher Marc-André Argentino puts it.

The boy allegedly had links to a network known as 764. Such groups are known to target young people in games including Roblox and Minecraft as well as communities struggling with mental health or sexual identity for online extortion, pressuring them into acts of violence and self-harm.

The 764 network, founded by a Texas teenager, Bradley Cadenhead, is just one part of an evolving online ecosystem, with perpetrators and victims in dozens of countries. Cadenhead is now serving an 80-year sentence in the US for possessing child sexual abuse material.

There are several cases currently before courts around the world with alleged links to such groups. Legal records from numerous countries suggest they often celebrate violence, manipulation and harm for its own sake, collecting records of such acts to gain notoriety and control.

“These are young people recruiting other young people,” says Bjørn Ihler, the founder of the security firm Revontulet. “It is a youth phenomenon.”

The Australian federal police commissioner, Krissy Barrett, has said: “A worrying trend is how victims are becoming perpetrators to try to escape their online bullies who have befriended and groomed them, and then forced them to hurt themselves.”

A Swedish court decided in April 2025 that the teenager had carried out the stabbing although he was too young to be held criminally responsible. But another name emerged during the investigation, local authorities told the Guardian – an online username: “Chai.”

In early 2025, as the country was still reeling from the attack, an Australian girl rang Swedish police. She wanted to tell authorities about Chai.

‘It’s bigger than these few cases’

Linus Svensson, an investigative reporter at the Swedish broadcaster SVT, had never heard of 764 before the 2024 stabbing.

Svensson says he now knows of at least nine local court cases related to “the Com” – the term for a broad online network that engages in cybercrime, extortion and violence, and which includes 764. He says he has found dozens of Swedish members in chat groups.

“It’s bigger than these few cases,” he says. “I think it took a while for Swedish authorities and also the general public to actually understand this.”

As he began to wade through videos and imagery shared by the group for SVT’s investigation, Svensson came across a teenager in the north of Sweden who had been convicted in 2024 of trying to coerce a 13-year-old boy to take his own life.

This, according to Jenny Östling, a senior public prosecutor with Sweden’s National Unit against International and Organised Crime, was Chai.

The teenager, whose real name cannot be published, is on trial for more than 70 alleged offences, according to the indictment, including allegedly encouraging someone to self-harm and kill themselves, and the creation of child sexual abuse material. Most were allegedly committed against the Australian girl.

He is also charged with inducing a young man in Germany to harm himself so badly he almost died.

His lawyer, Emily Töyrä, told the Guardian he denies all the allegations.

The trial was paused in late June after the Swedish court sent him for a forensic psychiatric investigation, according to court records, stating there was “compelling evidence that [he] has committed several of the acts with which he has been charged”. The matter will return in August.

Östling says the case will test whether people can be held responsible for remotely coercing others into acts of self-harm or violence – a hallmark of groups such as 764.

“They have a goal for the group itself: to destroy the world … But [members] also have a goal for themselves: they want to gain status within the group,” Östling says.

Creating new material can be a prerequisite of entry to closed chatrooms and other markers of membership. “They primarily coerce young victims into cutting themselves or sexual acts,” she says. “They use it to be able to coerce them into doing something worse.”

Östling alleges Chai was “high status” within 764, and was invited into a chatroom known as “764 Inferno”.

His lawyer disputes that characterisation, and says her client’s involvement was limited to editing images and videos. “The Com environment is highly fluid,” Töyrä says. “My client does not accept the characterisation of ‘764 Inferno’ as the type of organised group alleged by the prosecution. In his view, it was simply one group chat among many.”

A global phenomenon

An indictment unveiled by the US Department of Justice in April 2025 alleges that two American men in their early 20s, Leonidas Varagiannis and Prasan Nepal, were part of a chatroom with the same name which “was reserved for the inner core of 764 members”.

The pair are accused of using “764 Inferno” to conspire with other members to create and distribute child exploitation images, among other charges. Researchers have found at least 295 arrests linked to the Com network in 33 countries, including Australia, where there are matters before the courts.

In New Zealand, after a tipoff from US authorities, Ronndog Keefe pleaded guilty in 2025 to 13 charges, including the distribution of “horrific and graphic” child exploitation material. The 22-year-old was sentenced to more than five years’ jail in December.

Keefe claimed he was also a victim of 764, which he said had threatened to dox him if he did not distribute such material, according to legal records, but the court found this “simply was not credible”.

Last year in the UK, Cameron Finnigan, then 19, was given a nine-year extended sentence for possessing a terrorist document – a “kill guide” with advice about how to commit “truck attacks” – and indecent images of children. He was also convicted of encouraging someone online to take their own life.

The court found Finnigan was part of 764. “The intended victims are … vulnerable individuals: in particular, LGBTQI+ youth, racial minorities and those suffering from mental illnesses or disorders,” the judge said at his sentencing. “They are targeted precisely because they are so obviously vulnerable.”

In June another British teenager, Elijah Palmer, was sentenced for encouraging serious self-harm, among other charges. He was also linked to 764, police said, and had targeted his victim on Roblox and the chat platform Discord.

The FBI uses the term “nihilistic violent extremism” to describe these activities but there is debate about the moniker. Some argue it is vague and tries to unite too many different groups under one umbrella.

Researchers such as Argentino have noted that ideology in these spaces can be “fluid, performative, and primarily symbolic” – occult or neo-Nazi imagery can function as markers of group membership rather than “as coherent political programs”.

Membership is also vague, according to Bjørn Ihler, who prefers to add the term “misanthropic”. “These are basically Discord servers,” he says. “There’s channels upon channels upon channels.”

Ultimately, the pursuit of sextortion material is about “power and … control of the victim”, Ihler says, and such content can be shared in so-called “lore books” for further victimisation by others.

“Sharing those materials … leads to increased ‘clout’, which is like the social currency,” he says. “Grappling with that is incredibly important from a victim-protection perspective.”

‘It could happen to anyone’

Long before these arrests took place, an independent researcher, Becca Spinks, had been tracking these groups from her home in Texas.

“As a mom, I’m just horrified,” she says. “I couldn’t close my eyes and just be like, ‘Oh, well, someone else will deal with it.’ Who’s working on this? What’s going on? How can we help?”

As part of her work, she started to speak to the mother of Chai’s Australian alleged victim several years ago, who was looking for help to get the attention of authorities and assistance for her child.

The trials of men linked to 764 taking place all over the world, Spinks says, have come as some relief. “She’s very brave,” she says of the alleged victim in Chai’s case. “And her mum also is really just a powerhouse.”

Chai’s trial has largely taken place behind closed doors but the toll the alleged crimes have taken on victims is clear.

Spinks says her biggest priority is raising awareness for parents and law enforcement officials.

“A lot of times kids come forward and maybe [the police] don’t recognise the signs that it’s the 764 network, and so they don’t pursue it as aggressively as they should,” she says.

Spinks says there needs to be greater awareness for parents too. The Australian federal police cite warning signs including indications of self-harm, sudden withdrawal from family and friends and secretive behaviour about online interactions.

“One of the biggest, most dangerous misunderstandings is that this won’t happen to us, or this only happens to a certain type of kid, when in reality, it could honestly happen to anyone.”

title: Class X batch of 1983 at St. Aloysius High School gifts ₹65 lakh self-sustaining endowment
summary: The endowment is said to be the first-ever batch-led scholarship endowment of its kind in the 146-year-old institution
full_text:
The Class X batch of 1983 of St. Aloysius High School, Mangaluru, recently returned to their alma mater with a unique gift in the form of a self-sustaining scholarship endowment with an initial corpus of ₹65 lakh.

The endowment is said to be the first-ever batch-led scholarship endowment of its kind in the 146-year-old institution, according to a release. The endowment seeks to recognise students with outstanding academic promise while promoting the institute’s values of excellence and service.

The inaugural St. Aloysius Class of 1983 Scholarship Awards were recently held during the annual feast of St. Aloysius Gonzaga, the patron saint of youth and students. Scholarships were presented to Ashwini Shettigar, M.A. Abdul Azaz Shayan, Sharon D’Costa, and Snithik Churya.

On the occasion, retired assistant headmaster Shambu Shetty and retired primary school teachers Lidwin D’Souza and Celine Rego were felicitated for their lasting influence on the Class of 1983. Headmaster Fr. Johnson Pinto and Assistant Headmaster Lancy D’Souza were present. The Class of 1983 was represented by Anil Pinto, Rohan Mascarenhas, P. Sudhir, and Mahesh Nayak.

Mr. Shetty said, “It is easy to plant seeds. The real challenge is to nurture it and help it grow.” He urged the younger generation to carry the initiative forward and strengthen its legacy.

Self-sustaining endowment

The idea to award a scholarship was born in 2024, when over 70 classmates reunited through social media. What began as a nostalgic reunion soon grew into a shared vision. Months of planning with the institution followed. The endowment was formally established in April 2025 under the guidance of the then rector, late Fr. Melwyn Pinto.

The ₹65 lakh corpus is invested in carefully selected financial instruments under the guidance of classmates with expertise in finance. Only the annual investment earnings are used to fund scholarships, while the corpus remains intact and continues to grow through market returns and future contributions. The endowment is expected to benefit an increasing number of students from Class X to II PUC in the coming years. It is administered jointly by the alumni and the Institutional Development Office of St. Aloysius Institutions. Eom

title: From IAC to paper leaks: Why anti-system movements pose a unique political challenge | Explained
summary: The IAC movement consciously projected itself as a citizens’ campaign, even though the Congress-led UPA maintained that it represented a collaboration between the RSS and civil society activists
full_text:
The story so far: The student-led protests over recurring examination paper leaks and the conduct of the NEET examination have inevitably drawn comparisons with the India Against Corruption (IAC) movement that rattled the second United Progressive Alliance (UPA) government between 2011 and 2013.

The immediate triggers are different: corruption under the UPA and the credibility of public examinations under the National Democratic Alliance (NDA). Yet both movements display the potential to disrupt politics by presenting an outsider’s challenge to the political establishment.

Just as allegations of corruption came to symbolise perceived governance failure during the latter years of the Manmohan Singh government, recurring examination leaks have increasingly become a test of the BJP-led government’s promise of efficient and transparent governance.

Battle of narratives

Established parties carry ideological baggage, the trappings of power and electoral compulsions, making it difficult for them to convincingly channel public anger against the political system itself.

The IAC movement consciously projected itself as a citizens’ campaign, even though the Congress-led UPA maintained that it represented a collaboration between the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh and civil society activists. Regardless of the competing claims, the movement’s carefully crafted narrative of political independence enabled it to attract support cutting across ideological and social divides.

A similar dynamic is visible in the present agitation. Although Opposition parties have backed the students’ demands, the protests derive much of their legitimacy from remaining student-led rather than party-led, with innovator-turned-activist Sonam Wangchuk emerging as their principal public face.

Once a movement is seen as an extension of an Opposition party, governments can more easily dismiss it as routine political mobilisation instead of acknowledging it as an expression of wider public discontent.

It is perhaps for this reason that sections of BJP supporters have alleged that the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which has emerged as a principal force behind the students’ protests in Delhi, is being guided by the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP). CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke had earlier volunteered for AAP and worked with Manish Sisodia.

Whether or not such allegations are substantiated, they reflect a familiar political strategy: questioning a movement’s claim to independence by portraying it as a proxy for an established political rival. The Congress, meanwhile, has sought to remind students that it has been raising the issue of paper leaks “not for weeks or months but for years”. The contest, therefore, is not merely over paper leaks but also over who owns the political narrative.

The paradox of the system

Indian politics also illustrates the paradox of anti-establishment movements. Their moral authority stems from standing outside the political establishment, but translating public anger into policy ultimately requires entering the electoral arena.

The Assam Agitation culminated in the formation of the Asom Gana Parishad (AGP), which came to power in 1985 promising to redefine Assam’s politics. Over time, however, it became another participant in the conventional political system it had sought to transform.

AAP followed a similar trajectory. Born out of an anti-corruption movement, it built its identity around clean politics and accountability. Once in office, however, it found itself confronting allegations of corruption, particularly in the Delhi excise policy case, which the BJP used to question its anti-corruption credentials. AAP consistently maintained that the investigations were politically motivated.

Whatever the legal outcome of those cases, they underscored a larger political reality: once protest movements become governments, they are judged not by the standards of activism but by those of governance. Movements gain legitimacy by challenging the establishment, but enduring political influence often requires becoming part of it. In doing so, they inevitably become subject to the same scrutiny, compromises and accusations they once directed at those in power.

That is why every new anti-establishment movement is both politically disruptive and, eventually, politically vulnerable.

title: How Florida State University Is Building Its AI Ecosystem
summary:
Faculty and students, academic researchers, the staff and administrators working behind the scenes at colleges and universities around the country are all leveraging artificial intelligence to teach, learn, and work more efficiently and effectively.
One recent survey, in fact, found that 95% of students and educators are actively using AI tools. And while the surge in AI adoption in higher education kicked off in 2022 with OpenAI’s release of ChatGPT, today it’s being driven by a wide range of platforms from established and emerging companies alike.
In this environment, a growing number of…
full_text:
Partnerships Align With Campus Use Cases

For some institutions, the AI conversation eventually converges on a single trusted vendor, but FSU has decided to embrace the power of maintaining multiple partnerships.

“Our strategy has been to work with companies that are pushing the envelope on what could be in the world of AI,” explains Rebekah Dorn, the university’s chief experience and support officer. “We look for solutions that match our use cases, the AI tools that best fit those needs.”

Use cases are identified through structured pilot programs designed to let the campus community evaluate solutions and provide feedback. In a 2025 trial of Microsoft 365 Copilot, for example, graduate students in the university’s computer science program experimented with the tool to gain a better understanding of complex data sets. More recently, 30 instructors from departments across the university participated in a pilot called AI Sparks where they learned to use Google Gemini and NotebookLM for everything from literary analyses to creating mock interviews for business students.

DISCOVER: Institutions are facing a stability paradox when it comes to AI.

Faculty (Mostly) Lead the Way in Adoption

When it comes to the IT department’s role in deciding which AI vendors make the cut, “we’ve tried to put faculty in the driver’s seat,” says Robert Fuselier, chief academic technology officer. FSU’s technologists are “behind the scenes assessing these tools,” he explains, “but our biggest goal is to help faculty find ways to implement AI into their courses.”

The main caveat to this: Before an AI solution is introduced to the campus community, data protection agreements must be in place. “That’s, full-stop, the first thing we worry about,” says Dorn. “Only once we’re confident that we have a secure environment and that the vendor isn’t going to use our data to train other large language models do we let our faculty and staff get their hands on it.”

Adopting Multiple Tools Allows Users To Build AI Fluency

Today, FSU’s roster of AI tools licensed for student use includes Gemini, NotebookLM, Copilot, Zoom AI Companion and an AI-powered coaching service from LinkedIn Learning. Faculty and staff can use these solutions as well, and they also have access to Adobe Creative Cloud and CrowdStrike’s AI-enabled Falcon Complete Next-Gen managed detection and response cybersecurity service.

UP NEXT: AI adoption in higher ed requires careful security planning.

In addition, Dorn notes, the university recently launched a campuswide portal containing more than 100 large language models for academic and research purposes. Called ArtesAI, the cloud-based platform was built on Microsoft Azure and serves as a central hub for users to securely access and build custom AI tools while maintaining strict data privacy, she explains.

Finally, FSU’s Artificial Intelligence in Education Advisory Committee meets regularly to discuss how the technology has impacted teaching and learning, while its Artificial Intelligence Policy Workgroup is tasked with developing policies and guidance for responsible use of AI. Over time, Fuselier says, FSU hopes to improve AI fluency among students, with a goal of preparing FSU graduates for a future where AI solutions are nearly everywhere.

“It’s so important that they get experience with these tools while they’re here,” he says. “We know that they’re going to need these skills to be competitive in the workplace.”

title: AI, lifelong learning and inclusive higher education
summary: The post AI, lifelong learning and inclusive higher education appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Dr Inga Olari, Programme Leader in Law, explores how AI reshapes lifelong learning, inclusion, academic judgement and equity in universities.

AI and lifelong learning: promise or risk?

Artificial intelligence is no longer a future possibility for higher education; it is already reshaping how learners’ access, experience, and continue their education throughout life. The question is not simply whether universities should adopt AI, but whether they can do so responsibly without reproducing existing inequalities in new and more technical forms. The need for lifelong learning is increasing as automation, digital work, and professional change require adults to refresh their knowledge and skills throughout their careers. However, technology does not automatically create opportunity. Its value depends on how wisely institutions govern it, how inclusively they design it, and how carefully they protect the learners who may otherwise be left behind.

What AI can make possible

Thoughtfully, AI can be applied to an open learning process. Adaptive systems can accelerate things, propose resources, and provide quicker formative feedback. Learning analytics would help the employees to observe the student when he or she might need something, and when they were about to engage in non-confrontation by isolating themselves. Online micro-credentials and daily online modules may also help working adults, carers, and distance learners further their studies without quitting their jobs and family responsibilities. This is where AI can play the most significant part: it does not shut down universities but just frees the process and makes it more appropriate, timely, and personal. Having an immediate answer and convenient online support, out-of-school learners may reduce the amount of anxiety and support perseverance. In terms of institutions, they can reveal trends that would almost go undetected in cohorts that are large or dispersed.

Why inclusion cannot be assumed

The danger is that access can be mixed up with inclusion. Online and off-limits courses can occur when the students lack reliable devices, connectivity, quiet places to study, self-confidence, or computer skills. Students who are already prepared to navigate through academic and technological systems may be the ones who are most likely to benefit from AI-supported learning. In the absence of special focus, AI is more likely to increase than reduce gaps in participation. Beneath there are greater ethical issues. The algorithms that are trained using historical data can replicate prejudiced assumptions concerning ability, risk, and progress. Surveillance becomes possible when learning analytics are not in the eyes of the students, what information is captured, how it is processed, and by whom the action can be taken based on this information. Another domain that Generative AI is upsetting is assessment because low-understandable work can be obfuscated by the final products. That is why UNESCO (2023) believes that regulation ought to be people-centred and must engage in capacity-building and educational governance, rather than simply following.

The educator still matters

AI will not reduce the role of the educator but transform. Automated systems can facilitate routine feedback, whereas academic judgement, dialogue, ethical reasoning, or relationship building process to build confidence cannot. Learning throughout life cannot be a kind of funnel of competencies badges, which are labour-market oriented. Critical thinking, disciplinary depth, and civic purpose must still be guarded by universities. This means that the key one is staff development. To believe in AI, lecturers must be AI literate, but to distrust it. They must know what systems help to promote the learning process, where it is deformed, and they must know when they must analyse accepted human signals. Students should also be taught to use AI responsibly, as a ban on technologies does not contribute much to developing judgment; a properly designed interaction does.

What universities should do now

The moral is evident in the practical lesson. The institutions will have clear data practices, an open digital base, open design that is open-ended, employee training, and evaluation models that will pay off application, introspection, and resolution. The questions that they need to ask themselves when considering AI tools are: who wins and who loses; what is the evidence, and what human protections are provided? The concept of AI-assisted lifelong learning can be transformed into the direction towards a more balanced form of participation, which, nevertheless, remains not a priority among universities as an educational, rather than a technical, skill. Platforms are not going to be the future. It will be impacted by institutional choices on equity, trust, and purpose. So, how can higher education play a role in unlocking lifelong learning and protecting those learners whose lives are most negatively affected by the threat of being left behind by AI?

Dr Inga Olari is Programme Leader in Law for the Law Undergraduate Programmes with St Mary’s University Twickenham, and Fellow of the Association of Higher Education Professionals (AHEP). Her work focuses on legal education, inclusive pedagogy, AI in higher education, student success, and academic leadership. She has presented internationally on digital learning, lifelong learning, and culturally inclusive teaching practices

title: The new majority: Redesigning for the 25-45 adult learner
summary: Adult learners are becoming an increasingly important audience for higher education, but many university program pages still speak primarily to school leavers. Here's how to redesign your content, UX, and website experience for busy professionals who want clear answers, not a digital scavenger hunt.
full_text:
Adult learners often experience university websites differently from traditional undergraduate applicants, and it's why many program pages struggle to connect with an audience that higher education increasingly needs to reach.

Most university program pages were built with a fairly specific visitor in mind: an 18-year-old comparing colleges with help from parents, teachers, and guidance counsellors.

The challenge is that an increasing number of prospective students don't fit that profile.

They're already working. Some have children. Many have mortgages, rent payments, and calendars that leave very little room for browsing websites for fun.

As traditional-age student populations begin to decline in many regions, adult learners are becoming an increasingly important audience for colleges and universities.

Yet many program pages still speak primarily to school leavers rather than experienced professionals returning to education.

That's a missed opportunity.

The challenge is that many university websites still reflect how institutions are organised internally rather than how adult learners make decisions.

Adult learners don’t browse, they evaluate

A prospective undergraduate might happily spend an afternoon exploring campus videos, accommodation options, and student societies.

Adult learners are often working with much tighter constraints and have different priorities.

They're fitting research into lunch breaks, train journeys, and evenings after work.

And they're usually trying to answer a handful of practical questions before deciding whether it's worth investigating further.

They're not looking for information about residence halls or student clubs. They want to know whether a qualification will fit around their existing life.

How much will it cost? How long will it take? Can they study online? Will it help them move into a new role or progress in their current one?

These aren't new questions. What's changing is how many people are asking them.

If your program page makes those answers difficult to find, the visitor may never make it to the enquiry form.

Show people what success looks like

Many university program pages still open with sweeping hero campus photography, students walking between lectures, or carefully staged images of undergraduate life.

There's nothing wrong with that, but the problem is that it may not help an adult learner picture themselves in the story.

Someone researching an online master's degree after work isn't necessarily imagining life in student accommodation; they're imagining a promotion, a career change, a new opportunity.

So how can you change your imagery? You could use:

Graduates working in relevant industries

Adult learners balancing study and work

Alumni stories focused on career progression

Outcome-focused content that demonstrates where the qualification can lead

This way, you’re helping prospective students see a version of themselves in the future you're describing.

Don't make people hunt for answers

Many universities accidentally create a treasure hunt.

Cost information lives on one page. Entry requirements live somewhere else. Study options are hidden in a downloadable brochure. Start dates are buried three clicks deep.

Adult learners are unlikely to spend half an hour piecing everything together.

The most important information should be easy to find and easy to understand.

That includes:

Study format (online, hybrid, evening, weekend)

Expected duration

Tuition costs or cost ranges

Entry requirements

Upcoming start dates

Think about the last time you bought something online.

You probably expected to see the price before filling out a form.

Adult learners tend to approach program research in much the same way.

Put outcomes alongside modules

Universities are understandably proud of their curriculum.

Program pages often dedicate hundreds of words to modules, learning outcomes, and course structure.

Adult learners want that information too.

But they also want to understand where the qualification might take them.

That could include:

Graduate employment outcomes

Career pathways

Employer partnerships

Alumni success stories

Labour market demand data

For someone investing significant time and money, these aren't "nice to know" details.

They're often central to the decision-making process.

Remove friction wherever possible

Even strong content can be undermined by small frustrations.

Adult learners often browse on mobile devices during short windows of free time. They may be researching while commuting, waiting for an appointment, or catching up after work.

A few avoidable barriers can quickly become reasons to leave.

Take a look at your enquiry forms: Do you really need every field you're asking people to complete?

Review your mobile experience: Can somebody easily compare options, view costs, and submit a form using only their phone?

Look at your navigation: Can visitors quickly find online, part-time, or accelerated programs without opening multiple pages?

None of these changes are particularly dramatic.

Together, they can make a significant difference.

A simple exercise for this week

Open your three most visited program pages on your phone.

Now imagine you're a 38-year-old professional researching your options after dinner.

Without scrolling too far, can you answer these questions?

How much does this cost?

How long will it take?

Can I fit it around work?

What happens after graduation?

If not, you've probably identified an opportunity for improvement.

Meeting adult learners where they are

Universities have spent decades refining recruitment strategies for school leavers.

Many are now discovering that future growth may come from a broader audience.

Adult learners aren't looking for a completely different website.

They simply need a website that respects their time, answers practical questions, and makes it easy to understand whether a program is right for them.

Sometimes improving a program page isn't about adding more content.

It's about removing the small obstacles that get in the way of somebody taking the next step.

For an audience balancing careers, family commitments, and study ambitions, that can make all the difference.

How are you redesigning your adult learner pages? We'd love to hear about it.

title: What drives enrollment decisions today: Cost transparency
summary: Only 22% of Americans say the cost of getting a degree is worth it, even if you have to take out loans. In our research, cost-related concerns and financial aid discussions were consistent—students and families want a clear understanding of the cost and to know the degree is worth their investment.
full_text:
Only 22% of Americans say the cost of getting a degree is worth it, even if you have to take out loans. In our research, cost-related concerns and financial aid discussions were consistent—students and families want a clear understanding of the cost and to know the degree is worth their investment.

A partnership with Jeff Selingo for his book Dream School: Finding the College That’s Right For You, prompted us to explore recent online college admissions conversation. The insights and themes we uncovered prompted us to return to our analyses of the college decision-making journey over the past ten years.

Jeff Selingo’s book guides students and families to look beyond elite schools by identifying seven measurable dimensions of a “good school” that most rankings don’t capture. Campus Sonar developed actionable strategies from our research to help campuses improve their student-centric approach by focusing on recruiting and enrolling students based on individual fit, ensuring future success for students and sustainable institutions.

Actionable strategy

Explain costs transparently

In this 10-year data set, cost-related concerns peaked in March of 2024, primarily due to the FAFSA processing delays. Prospective students want affordable options that don't require student loans, prompting them to include community colleges and trade schools in a decision set where previously they only included four-year institutions.

Cost remains the leading factor in college decision-making. It’s critical to explain costs transparently in many ways, in many more spaces than you currently do. Communicate costs in ways that align with your institution's goals and don't undermine your financial goals, but meet families where they are.

Campus Sonar’s recommendation is to make sure students and families clearly understand what they’re paying compared to the value they receive. They want their real-life pain points of increasing tuition and decreasing financial aid addressed so they can confidently make the college decision.

Take action: Actively address pain points

Understand the pain points, weaknesses, and barriers to the financial aid and enrollment processes and address them actively, consistently, and clearly.

A medium-sized private college in the East wanted to understand the perception of their brand, build awareness, and strengthen their reputation.

Strategic support

Differentiate your campus by communicating college costs and associated value with realism and transparency.
